items.proposition: Delhi Rent Control Act section 14(1)(b) supplies the controlling statutory candidate: where, on or after 9 June 1952, the tenant sub-lets, assigns, or otherwise parts with possession of the whole or any part of the premises without the landlord's written consent, the Controller may order recovery of possession. Section 16 reinforces the written-consent requirement for post-1952 subletting and for post-commencement subletting, transfer, or assignment.

evidence.quote: (b) that the tenant has, on or after the 9th day of June, 1952, sub-let, assigned or otherwise parted with the possession of the whole or any part of the premises without obtaining the consent in writing of the landlord;

(2) No premises which have been sub-let either in whole or in part on or after the 9th day of June, 1952, without obtaining the consent in writing of the landlord, shall be deemed to have been lawfully sub-let.

items.relevance: The target petition is expressly under Delhi section 14(1)(b), and the alleged conduct is said to have occurred after 9 June 1952 without written consent. The statutory text therefore supplies the direct legal ground against which the alleged parting with possession must be assessed.
items.limits: The supplied statutory texts are Indian Kanoon statutory reproductions whose historical version as of the target date is unverified and are not an authenticated historical consolidation or Official Gazette text. They contain no judicial definition of what factual circumstances constitute 'parted with the possession.'
items.review_reason: One model-assisted review of original unit text confirms the stated proposition and limited role. The Delhi statute is a version-limited reproduction; GR reported Delhi is a report of precedent, not its full opinion. For bank succession, TS remains prima facie/reserved and GR an AP-law analogy, not a Delhi holding. Unlocated model quotation strings are retained as quotation defects; reviewer anchors below point to the unaltered source, not a silently repaired quotation.

items.proposition: Within the allowed target record, the operative dispute was narrowed away from subletting and to whether Duli Chand had parted with possession; the tenant had not pleaded that he obtained written consent from the landlord for such parting.

evidence.quote: the tenant-Duli Chand has sub:let or parted with the possession of the said shop after 9th day of June, 1952 to M/s Hira Lal Sri Bhagwan illegally and without the written consent of the landlord.

On the facts and circumstances of the case, the question of subletting did not arise but the case was considered on the dispute whether the tenant had parted with possession of the shop. The tenant never pleaded that he had obtained any written consent from the landlord for parting with posses- sion.

items.relevance: This fixes the section 14(1)(b) branch that matters on the supplied record: parting with possession, with written consent unavailable as a pleaded defence.
items.limits: This is issue framing from the allowed target record, not the withheld Supreme Court final reasoning or outcome. It does not itself establish the legal meaning of parting with possession.
items.review_reason: Contains target-record IDs rather than an all-library legal-source bundle. Retained as qualitative analysis, not converted into invented legal units or a legal retrieval denominator.

items.proposition: The Rent Control Tribunal, followed by the High Court, treated the tenant as having parted with legal possession. Their accepted factual findings included that Sri Bhagwan alone owned the business operating from the premises, was in exclusive possession, Duli Chand had no interest in that business, worked at another shop, had neither pleaded concurrent use nor a licence, and had retained no control despite occasionally being seen at the shop.

evidence.quote: On appeal by the landlord the Rent Control Tribunal held that the tenant had parted with the legal possession of the tenanted premises and in that view ordered the eviction of the tenant under section 14(1)(b) of the Act.
The second appeal filed by the tenant to the High Court was dismissed confirming the finding of the Rent Control Tribunal that the tenant had parted with possession of the tenanted shop.

Sri Bhagwan is in exclusive possession of the property, that tenant Duli Chand works at another Shop, M/s Aggarwal Hard- ware and Mills Stores with his younger son, that there was no plea of concurrent user of the premises by the tenant nor there is any plea that Sri Bhagwan is a licensee, that occasionally the tenant-Duli Chand was seen sitting in the shop and that the tenant had not retained any control over the same.

items.relevance: Exclusive possession by another person, absence of the tenant's business interest, work elsewhere, and lack of retained control are the principal supplied facts capable of supporting the statutory allegation that possession was parted with. The Tribunal and High Court also actually adopted that characterization.
items.limits: The Rent Controller had reached the opposite result, and the target Supreme Court's final treatment of the findings is withheld. The supplied legal library does not provide a direct Delhi section 14(1)(b) test establishing that these particular facts necessarily constitute legal parting with possession.

items.proposition: The tenant opposed the inference of parting by asserting that Sri Bhagwan was his son, that possession remained with the tenant, and that merely permitting his son to conduct business could not amount to parting with legal possession. He also disputed the landlord's adoption theory, invoking a Supreme Court adoption rule requiring a formal giving-and-taking ceremony and asserting that evidence of a valid adoption was absent.

evidence.quote: He further pleaded that the possession of the shop is with the tenant.

The learned counsel for the appellant, however, contend- ed that Sri Bhagwan was not the adopted son of Hira Lal and that by permitting the son to carry on business it could not be stated that he had 469 parted with the legal possession of the premises.

wherein this Court had held that in order that an adoption may be valid under Hindu Law there must be a formal ceremony of giving and taking by the natural parent and the adopted parent after exercising their volition to give and take the boy in adoption and that such an evidence of a valid adoption is not available in this case.

items.relevance: The family relationship and disputed adoption bear on the landlord's characterization of Sri Bhagwan as a separate possessor and provide the principal supplied counterargument to the inference drawn from his occupation of the shop.
items.limits: The reported Lakshman Singh Kothari proposition concerns validity of adoption under Hindu law, not the Delhi Rent Control Act test for parting with possession. The full Lakshman opinion is not supplied, and even failure to prove adoption does not by itself determine whether Duli Chand retained legal possession or control.

items.proposition: A 1986 Supreme Court authority in the supplied library reports the earlier Parasaram decision as construing Delhi Rent Control Act section 14(b) broadly enough to cover not only subleases but assignments and any other mode by which possession of the tenanted premises is parted, including an involuntary sale.

evidence.quote: This Court held that the amplitude of S. 14(b) of the Delhi Rent Control Act was wide enough not only to include any sublease but even an assignment or any other mode by which possession of the tenanted premises is parted. In view of the wide amplitude of s. 14(b), it does not exclude even an involuntary sale.

items.relevance: This supports a broad reading of the statutory alternatives and confirms that 'otherwise parted with possession' is not confined to a conventional sublease. It therefore supports treating the target's possession issue as independently cognizable even though the target record states that subletting itself did not arise.
items.limits: The unit is General Radio's report of Parasaram, not an independently supplied full Parasaram opinion. Its described facts concern liquidation and sale of tenancy rights, not a tenant's son operating a sole-proprietary business from the premises. It establishes breadth of the provision but does not supply a fact-specific test for retained control or family occupation.

items.proposition: In a 1980 Delhi High Court company-amalgamation setting, the court expressed only a prima facie view that tenancy vesting through an amalgamation order might not require landlord consent and might lie outside section 14(1)(b), while expressly reserving whether such a transfer nevertheless amounted to an assignment attracting eviction and preserving the landlord's right to pursue that issue before the appropriate forum.

evidence.quote: Prima facie, the rights of the transferor-company in the tenancy, contractual or statutory, are transferable on an amalgamation by virtue of the vesting order to be made by the court while sanctioning the scheme of amalgamation or thereafter and having regard to the nature of such a vesting it would not require the consent of the landlord and would be outside the mischief of the provisions of s. 14(1)(b) of the Rent Control Act.

This court is, however, not concerned at this stage if the transfer by or consequent on amalgamation by the order of the court would nevertheless be tantamount to the assignment of a tenancy and if without the consent of the landlord would render the company or the transferee-company liable to eviction under s. 14(1)(b) of the Rent Control Act or otherwise be actionable in a regular civil action against them.

items.relevance: The unit cautions that some legally compelled or court-ordered vesting contexts can complicate a simple inference from transfer to section 14(1)(b) liability, and it illustrates the importance of the precise legal character of the transfer.
items.limits: The view was expressly prima facie and the section 14(1)(b) eviction question was reserved. The context was a company amalgamation and court vesting, which is materially different from the target's alleged transfer of possession to the tenant's son; it therefore provides no direct defence on the target facts.
items.review_reason: Main proposition is supported with the recorded scope limits, but its inclusion as a useful legal reference for this non-amalgamation target is disputable. Full source/quotation defects retained; exclude from primary denominator and include symmetrically in sensitivity analysis.

analysis_points: The direct statutory candidate requires a post-9 June 1952 subletting, assignment, or other parting with possession of the whole or part of the premises without written landlord consent. On the allowed target record, the proceeding was narrowed to parting with possession, and the tenant had not pleaded written consent.

The strongest supplied factual support for the ground is the Tribunal/High Court finding that Sri Bhagwan exclusively possessed the premises as sole proprietor of the business, while Duli Chand had no business interest there, worked elsewhere, pleaded neither concurrent use nor licence, and retained no control beyond occasional presence.

There is a genuine conflict in the prior adjudicative record: the Rent Controller found that parting with possession was not proved, while the Tribunal found legal parting and the High Court confirmed that finding. The withheld Supreme Court reasoning cannot be supplied or inferred to resolve that conflict.

The supplied Parasaram report supports a broad conception of section 14(b), extending beyond conventional subletting to assignment and other modes of parting with possession. It does not, however, provide the missing fact-specific rule for determining when a parent has legally parted with possession by allowing a son to operate a business in the premises.

Accordingly, the supplied materials give substantial support to the section 14(1)(b) ground if the accepted findings of Sri Bhagwan's exclusive possession and Duli Chand's lack of retained control satisfy the legal concept of parting with possession. The source set does not contain enough direct interpretive law to convert that conditional assessment into a definitive reconstruction of the withheld final outcome.
gaps: The target Supreme Court's final reasoning and final outcome are expressly excluded, so the source set cannot establish how that Court ultimately treated the prior findings.

No supplied Delhi authority directly defines the controlling test for 'parted with the possession' or 'legal possession' in the specific situation where an adult son operates a separate sole-proprietary business from the tenanted premises while the tenant is only occasionally present.

The full Parasaram opinion is not supplied; only General Radio's report of its broad section 14(b) holding is available. The full Lakshman Singh Kothari opinion is likewise not supplied, and the target record reports it only for adoption law.

The Delhi statutory reproductions are current-snapshot materials with historical versions unverified, so the library does not independently authenticate the precise statutory consolidation operative on 8 December 1989.

The record states that the tenant never pleaded written consent, but it does not supply a separate consent instrument or a complete evidentiary record independently establishing all circumstances of possession and control.
disputes: The Rent Controller found that the landlord had not proved parting with possession, whereas the Rent Control Tribunal found that Duli Chand had parted with legal possession and the High Court confirmed that finding.

The landlord alleged that Sri Bhagwan, although Duli Chand's natural son, had been adopted by Hira Lal and had thereby gone out of Duli Chand's family; the tenant disputed a valid adoption and relied on the absence of evidence of the required formal giving-and-taking ceremony.

The tenant maintained that possession remained with him and argued that permitting his son to conduct business did not amount to parting with legal possession, while the Tribunal/High Court findings described Sri Bhagwan as being in exclusive possession and Duli Chand as retaining no control.
